subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 1 of Year 2 Computing at Ehel Academy. The unit is called “Be a Game Developer”, but the big idea underneath the fun title is two words: algorithms and programs. An algorithm is a set of clear, step-by-step instructions, in the right order, for doing a job. A program is a set of instructions that a computer can follow.

Getting dressed, tidying their toys, or helping to make anjero are all algorithms — steps done in the right order. We start from these everyday steps and slowly give you the computing words for what they already do.

There are three big ideas in this unit. First, an algorithm must be precise — that means exact, clear and correct. “Move” is not precise; “Move 4 steps forward” is precise. Second, programs tell computers what to do, and a computer follows the steps exactly because a computer cannot think for itself. Third, we can turn an algorithm into a program by changing each step into a block of code, and then run it.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: These come straight from the textbook unit. By the end of the unit, the child should be able to:
Know that an algorithm is a precise set of instructions in the right order.
Know that programs tell computers what to do, and that a computer follows them exactly.
Turn an algorithm into a program by changing each step into a block of code.
Write and run a simple program in ScratchJr.

concepts.title: What is an algorithm? Giving clear instructions
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of steps for doing a job. For the steps to work, each instruction must be clear — it must say exactly what to do. A fuzzy instruction like “Move” leaves you guessing; a clear one like “Take 4 steps forward” does not.

Simon says take 4 steps forward. Simon says move. Why did everyone do something different when I just said 'move'? Because 'move' does not tell us enough!
concepts.example: A good instruction tells us exactly what to do. Play a quick game of Simon Says to start.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put a few everyday steps into a sensible order? Can you tell a clear instruction from a fuzzy one?

concepts.title: Be precise, and get the order right
concepts.explanation:
There is a special computing word for a clear instruction: precise. Precise means exact, clear and correct. An algorithm works best when every step is precise AND the steps are in the right order. If the order is wrong, even good steps give a silly result.

Watch — I will put my shoe on first, then my sock on top. All the steps are here, but the order is silly! Order matters. Precise is our new word.
concepts.example: It means exact and clear. Let us find the precise instructions.
concepts.checkYourself: it say exactly. Can you put steps in a sensible order? Praise careful thinking over speed.

concepts.title: Programs: instructions a computer follows
concepts.explanation:
A program is a set of instructions that a computer can follow. A computer is a machine — it cannot think for itself, so it does exactly what the program says, no more and no less. That is why the instructions in a program must be precise.

The robot may only do exactly what it is told. Robot, take 3 steps forward. Now turn right. Now stop. go over there.
concepts.example: You just gave the robot a program! A computer works just like our robot — it follows your steps exactly and cannot guess.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know a computer game is a program? Can you match a simple block to its job?

concepts.title: Making a program in ScratchJr (the Whale spins)
concepts.explanation:
Now we turn an algorithm into a real program in ScratchJr, using four easy steps: (1) break the task into small parts — a background, a character, and one action; (2) write the algorithm; (3) change each step into a block of code; (4) run it. Our task: make the Whale do one full spin.

our picture instructions. our GO button — we tap it to run the program. Open ScratchJr on a big tablet.
concepts.example: Find one real example of making a program in ScratchJr (the Whale spins) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tap the green flag to run it? Can you find a block by its colour and drag it to join the others?

concepts.title: More blocks: talk and hop; build and run
concepts.explanation:
A program can have more than one action. We add two new blocks: the Say block (purple — it shows a speech bubble so the character can talk) and the Hop block (blue — it makes the character jump up). We build a slightly longer program, then run it and check it matches our algorithm.

Blue blocks move, purple blocks talk. First the algorithm
concepts.example: Find one real example of more blocks: talk and hop; build and run around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you use the Say block and type or pick a short message? Can you test your program by tapping it, and check it matches what you planned? Can you add and join more than two blocks in the right order?

debugging.symptom: The order does not matter as long as all the steps are there.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: All the steps are there, but the order is silly. Order is part of the algorithm. Point it out: put your shoes on, then your socks on top.

debugging.symptom: The computer knows what I mean.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: A computer cannot guess or think — it only does exactly what the blocks say. Use the Robot Game: when you give a fuzzy instruction, the robot freezes.

debugging.symptom: A computer game just happens by magic.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Every game is a program that a person wrote, step by step. This is a lovely, empowering idea for them — people made it, so people like them can make one too.

debugging.symptom: Any turn number will spin it around.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: In ScratchJr the number matters: a turn of 3 is only a quarter turn. It takes 12 to go all the way around once. If a spin looks wrong, check the number.

debugging.symptom: Blocks work even if they are not joined.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Blocks must click together in a row, like a jigsaw, or only the first one runs. Confusing 'Start on Green Flag' and 'Start on Tap'. Green flag blocks run when you tap the green flag at the top; tap blocks run when you tap the character itself. If nothing happens, check which start block is on top.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

project.title: Unit 1 Project: Be a Game Developer
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Game Developer into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a game developer project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: My Pilot moves up, spins, and moves across when I tap it.
My other character says "Help!", hops, and moves.
I tapped my character to run the program, and it worked!
